items.title: George Avakian interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 21, 1998
items.q: he was the man who hired me to do that great series of the Hot Jazz Classics reissues

ctx.x: Oh that was a kind of an interesting thing because I was already aware of what was beginning to happen before the war. You see I got drafted straight off the campus, I was inducted about two or three months after I graduated from Yale. The first inkling was in the form of Dizzy Gillespie’s playing. And I first heard Dizzy in I guess it was 1938 because I remember discussing it with Marshall Stearns. His records came out and there were solos of Dizzy’s on various releases, including of course the Cab Calloway…

items.q: The upshot was that Mr. Wallerstein asked me to come to Columbia once a week.

ctx.x: Anyway, within a short time of the completion of the Chicago Jazz album, an unexpected development took place, which was the beginning of my association with Columbia Records. In early 1940, there was a substantial amount of public interest in the form of things like a spread in Life magazine, which was the magazine of the time, covering a kind of history of jazz. It surprised all of us by having pictures of people like Bix Beiderbecke and so on. There’s that famous big photograph that was taken on a Harlem…
